transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I suppose what brings me in is that, for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around the house. Fixing things, arranging the pantry, volunteering for just one more thing at the church... even at 87, I have a terrible time just sitting down and being still. 

It’s funny, I was trying to watch Jeopardy last night—I still miss Alex Trebek, you know, he had such a comforting voice. My late husband and I used to watch him every single evening on this dreadful green floral sofa we bought at a Sears back in the eighties. That Sears is a mattress store now, if you can believe it. They just tear everything down these days. But anyway, I couldn't even sit through Final Jeopardy without getting up to dust the mantelpiece! I just always have to be doing something, and my daughter thought maybe I should talk to someone about it.
When you feel like you can't sit still, is it because you're feeling worried or anxious about something, or more because you're feeling unusually energetic, upbeat, or 'wired'?

Goodness, no, I don't think I'm worried. Well, I mean, I worry about normal things. Like my grandson, David—he just bought one of those electric scooters, and I read in the Sunday paper that the batteries on those things can just catch fire! Can you imagine? Just bursting into flames right there in the garage. I told my daughter she needs to make him keep it outside, but she never listens to me. She gets that stubbornness from her father's side, bless his heart. 

But no, it's not worry that makes me get up and dust the mantel. And I certainly wouldn't say I'm "wired" or unusually energetic. I'm 87! I haven't been wired since... well, maybe when they used to put real sugar in Coca-Cola. Oh, the little glass bottles were so much better, weren't they? Now everything is plastic and it just tastes like a factory. I stopped drinking it altogether in the nineties. 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right. No, I don't feel anxious or upbeat when it happens. I just... I don't really know why I do it. I just feel like my hands and feet need to be busy, even when I'm perfectly content.
Have you or your family noticed any recent problems with your memory—like forgetting recent conversations, misplacing things more often, or getting confused about dates or directions?

Well, memory... no, I wouldn't say my memory is going. I mean, my daughter hasn't said anything about it. She's always so quick to point out if I've done something wrong, you know. Just last week, she came over and saw I had reorganized the spice rack alphabetically instead of by cuisine, and she made this little huffing sound. She does that exact same huff her father used to do when I'd suggest we stop and ask for directions. 

We took this trip to Mount Rushmore back in '76—the bicentennial year, you know. Everyone was wearing those awful polyester pantsuits in red, white, and blue. I had a lovely navy one, actually, with little anchor buttons. But anyway, he refused to pull over in South Dakota, and we ended up at some roadside attraction with a giant prairie dog made of concrete. It was the strangest thing. They sold these little bags of saltwater taffy that were hard as rocks. I chipped a tooth on a peppermint one and had to see a dentist in Rapid City. He had the thickest mustache I've ever seen on a man. 

But no, I don't think I'm getting confused about dates or forgetting things. I remember that prairie dog perfectly! I just... I just have a lot of energy, that's all.
Have you noticed any recent weight loss, feeling unusually warm or sweaty, or a racing heartbeat lately?

Weight loss? Oh, heavens no. If anything, I've put on a pound or two since the holidays. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house with the hydrangeas that always look a bit wilted—she brought over this fruitcake. Now, normally I can't stand fruitcake. It's just heavy and tastes like old perfume. But hers had these little candied cherries that reminded me of the ones my mother used to put in her icebox cookies. 

We used to have this big, clunky Frigidaire when I was a girl. The handle was so heavy you had to use two hands to pull it open. My brother Tommy once got his tie caught in the door right before church. Oh, he was so mad! Mother had to cut it with her sewing shears. It was his favorite tie, too—a horrible mustard yellow thing with little brown ducks on it. I don't know why boys wear such ugly things when they're teenagers. 

But no, I'm not losing weight. And I haven't been sweaty or had my heart race, either. My heart is just fine. I get my blood pressure checked at the pharmacy when I pick up my eye drops, and the machine always says it's perfectly normal. Though those machines are so loud, aren't they? They squeeze your arm so tight I always think it's going to pop right off like a doll's arm. But no, none of that. I just can't sit still!
Have you or your daughter noticed any new difficulty keeping up with things like paying bills, managing your medications, or remembering appointments?

Bills? Oh heavens, no. I pay my bills the very day they come in the mail. I still write paper checks, you know. My daughter is always pestering me to do it on the iPad, but I just don't trust it. The internet is just floating around in the air, it feels like anyone could just reach up and grab your bank account right out of the sky! I like to sit at my kitchen table with a good pen. I only use blue ink. Black ink always looks so severe, like a collection notice. 

I went to the post office just Tuesday to get a new book of stamps for my envelopes, and they gave me these ones with... oh, what were they... sea cows! Manatees, that's it. Just big gray blobs floating in the water. I asked the clerk—it was a new girl, not Susan. Susan retired to Florida last year to be near her sister who had that terrible hip replacement. Anyway, I asked the new girl if they had any nice flowers or flags, and she just looked at me like I was speaking Greek. Young people today just don't appreciate a pretty piece of mail. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, keeping up with things. No, I don't have any trouble. I write all my doctor appointments on the big calendar on the fridge, right next to the grocery list. And my medications are all sorted in one of those plastic boxes with the little lids that snap shut for the days of the week. Though the 'T' and the 'W' are starting to rub off on mine... I should probably get a new one. Maybe I'll ask David to drive me to the pharmacy later. 

But no, no trouble at all with my memory or my chores. I'm sharp as a tack! I just have these fidgety hands and feet that want to be doing something.
Can you tell me about all the medications you're currently taking, including any new prescriptions or over-the-counter drugs you started in the past year?

Medications? Oh, let's see... no, I don't think I take anything at all. No prescriptions, no. I've always been very healthy, praise the Lord. My mother was the same way, you know. She lived to be ninety-two and never took so much as an aspirin. She swore by a hot cup of lemon water every morning and a brisk walk. 

We used to walk down to the bakery on Elm Street. Oh, the smell of that place! They made these little almond cookies that were just heavenly. The baker, Mr. Rossi, was this big, booming Italian man who always wore a white apron covered in flour. He had a parrot in the shop, if you can believe it. A bright green thing that would squawk "Fresh bread! Fresh bread!" whenever the bell above the door rang. I always wondered if it was sanitary, having a bird right there near the pastries, but nobody seemed to mind back then. Things were so different. 

Now, you go into a bakery and everything is wrapped in plastic, and the girls behind the counter look at their phones the whole time. It's just a shame. But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, pills. No, I don't take any. Just a daily vitamin, maybe, when I remember to buy them. But no real medicine. I just have all this pep!
Does this restless, need-to-move feeling mainly involve your legs, and does it tend to get worse in the evening or when you're sitting still, then feel better once you get up and move around?

My legs? Oh, no, it's not just my legs. It's my hands, my arms, my whole body just feels like a motor is running inside me! I don't know about the evening... I feel like this all day long, really. Sitting still is just impossible, whether it's morning, noon, or night. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to sit and watch that nice game show, the one with the spinning wheel? Pat Sajak, he's always so charming. Though I do think Vanna White's dresses have gotten a bit too flashy lately. Back in the eighties, she wore such elegant gowns. My sister Margaret had a dress just like one Vanna wore in 1986—a lovely emerald green silk with a sweetheart neckline. She wore it to her daughter's wedding. 

Oh, that wedding! It was in this beautiful old church with stained glass windows that looked like spun sugar when the sun hit them. But the reception, well, they had a chocolate fountain. A fountain! Can you imagine? Some little boy stuck his whole hand right in it and then wiped it on the white linen tablecloths. His mother was mortified. She was wearing this awful peach pantsuit that just washed her right out. Peach is such a hard color to wear. You really need the right complexion for it. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, moving around. Yes, getting up doesn't really make it go away. I just feel like I need to be doing something constantly. Even when I'm up and walking, I'm tapping my fingers or humming a tune. It's just a constant buzzing feeling everywhere!
Over the past year, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy—along with this restless feeling?

Sad? Oh, heavens no. I haven't been sad at all. If anything, I'm just too full of beans! I haven't lost interest in anything, either. I still love my gardening. I was just out there this morning pulling up weeds around the hydrangeas. 

Hydrangeas are such funny plants, aren't they? You know, you can change the color of the blooms just by putting things in the soil. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house on the corner with the terrible vinyl siding—she puts rusty nails in her soil to make her hydrangeas blue! I told her that sounds like a good way to get lockjaw if you aren't careful with your trowel, but she swears by it. I prefer pink, myself. Pink is such a cheerful color. I had a pink sweater set in the fifties that was just darling. It had these little pearl buttons down the front. I wore it when I met my husband, actually! We were at a church picnic, and he was trying to carry three plates of potato salad at once. 

He dropped one right on my nice white Keds! But he was so apologetic, and he had the bluest eyes... just like Paul Newman. Did you ever see that movie with Paul Newman, the one with the bicycles? Or was it cars? He liked cars, didn't he? He had his own salad dressing, too. I buy the vinaigrette sometimes, it's very tangy. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my mood. No, no, I'm not down in the dumps at all. I just can't seem to stop going and going and going!
Over this past year, have you noticed any change in how much sleep you need—like feeling fully rested after only four or five hours, or finding you just don't need as much sleep as you used to?

Sleep? Oh, well... I've always been a good sleeper, really. I don't think I need any less sleep now than I did before. I still try to get my full eight hours. I like to be in bed by ten o'clock sharp, right after the local news. 

The news is so depressing these days, though, isn't it? It's all just crime and politics. I miss the days when they'd show a nice story about a cat stuck in a tree, and the firemen coming to get it down. Firemen are always so handsome, aren't they? My cousin, Jimmy, he was a fireman back in Chicago. He had this big, thick mustache. All the men had mustaches back then, it was the style! It looked like a caterpillar was resting on his upper lip, I used to tell him. He hated when I said that. 

He married a girl named Betty who made the most wonderful cherry pie. She used real tart cherries, not that syrupy canned stuff. You have to use the tart ones or it's just too sweet. She won a blue ribbon at the state fair for it in 1974. Or was it '75? No, it was '74 because that was the year we had that terrible blizzard and we were snowed in for three days! We just sat around playing Pinochle and eating cherry pie. I never want to see another hand of Pinochle as long as I live! 

But what was the question? Oh, sleep. Yes, I still sleep just fine. I don't wake up feeling like I only need four hours or anything like that. I just... wake up and start buzzing!
Have you noticed your thoughts feeling like they're racing or jumping quickly from one idea to another, or that it's hard to keep your mind focused on one thing lately?

Racing thoughts? Well, I don't know if I'd say racing, exactly. I mean, my mind is always busy, of course. There's always something to think about! Like this morning, I was thinking about whether I should make a pot roast for Sunday dinner. 

A good pot roast takes time, you know. You have to sear the meat first to lock in the juices. My mother taught me that. She used this heavy cast-iron skillet that weighed an absolute ton. I don't know how she lifted it, she was such a tiny woman! Barely five feet tall in her stocking feet. She used to buy her shoes in the children's department because her feet were so small. They had these little Mary Janes with a strap across the top... I always wanted a pair like that, but my feet were too wide. 

I had to wear these clunky oxfords when I was a girl. They were so sturdy, they felt like wearing bricks! But my father insisted. He said you needed good arch support or your feet would fall flat as pancakes by the time you were thirty. He was a podiatrist, you see. Dr. Arthur Pendleton. Everyone in town went to him for their corns and bunions. He had this big jar of peppermints on his desk for the children, but they were those chalky ones that tasted like toothpaste. I always preferred butterscotch, myself. Those little yellow candies wrapped in cellophane... they just melt in your mouth! 

But what were we talking about? Oh, my mind jumping around. Well, I suppose I do think about a lot of things, but I wouldn't say my thoughts are racing or out of control. I'm just... thinking! There's just so much to remember, isn't there?
Do you drink coffee, tea, or any caffeinated beverages, or take any herbal supplements or energy-boosting products on a regular basis?

Coffee? Oh, my, no. I haven't had a cup of coffee since... well, it must be twenty years now. It always gave me the most terrible heartburn! And tea, well, I'll have a cup of chamomile before bed sometimes, but that doesn't have any of that caffeine in it. It's very soothing. 

Chamomile reminds me of my Aunt Clara. She used to grow it in her herb garden out back. She had this beautiful little cottage with a thatched roof—can you imagine, a thatched roof in Ohio? The neighbors thought she was absolutely eccentric. She used to dry the herbs by hanging them upside down from the rafters in her kitchen. The whole house smelled like a meadow! She had a parrot, too, named Captain Flint. Oh, that bird was a menace! He used to mimic the sound of the telephone ringing, and poor Aunt Clara would go rushing into the hallway, wiping her hands on her apron, only to find nobody on the line. 

Telephones used to be so heavy, didn't they? The ones with the rotary dial. It took forever to call anyone if they had a lot of nines or zeroes in their number! Click, click, click... and if your finger slipped, you had to hang up and start all over again! Now everyone has those little glass rectangles they poke at. My grandson got me one for Christmas, but I can never remember how to answer it when it rings. It just buzzes and flashes at me like a very angry firefly. 

But what was I saying? Oh, right, caffeine and things. No, I don't take any of those energy things or supplements. Goodness, with how much I'm always buzzing around these days, if I took an energy pill, I think I'd just launch right up into orbit!

Doctor: What about other medical conditions—have you been diagnosed with anything else, like a thyroid problem or any other physical illness, recently?

Patient: Thyroid? Oh, let me think... no, I don't believe so. Dr. Henderson always checks my blood pressure, though. He has one of those new electronic cuffs, not the old ones where they had to pump the little rubber bulb. 

My husband, Harold, rest his soul, he hated getting his blood pressure taken. He said it squeezed his arm too tight. Harold was a stubborn man, bless him. He wouldn't go to the doctor unless he was practically on his deathbed! He worked at the lumber yard for forty-five years. Carried those heavy planks all day long. He had arms like Popeye, I used to tell him! We used to watch Popeye on Saturday mornings with the children. 

Cartoons just aren't the same anymore, are they? Now they're all computer-generated and so loud! The colors give me a headache. Back then, they were drawn by hand. It must have taken hours and hours just to make one little scene. I tried my hand at drawing once, took a watercolor class at the community center in... oh, must have been 1982. The instructor was a lovely woman named Beatrice. She wore these big, colorful silk scarves draped over her shoulders. She looked very bohemian. I painted a bowl of fruit, but the bananas came out looking like yellow sausages! We had such a good laugh over that. 

But what was it you asked? Oh, illnesses. No, no new illnesses or thyroid things. I'm healthy as a horse, really, aside from just not being able to sit still!

Soreness? Or being tired and irritable? Oh, goodness no. If anything, I have too much energy! I certainly don't feel tired. Just yesterday I was up in the attic sorting through some old boxes. You wouldn't believe the dust up there! 

I actually found my old Singer sewing machine tucked away in a corner. It's one of those beautiful, heavy black ones with the gold filigree painted on the side. They really don't make things to last anymore, do they? Everything you buy nowadays is just cheap plastic that breaks in a year. But that Singer, oh, it runs like a dream. I used to sew all of my daughter Susan's dresses on that machine. She had this one favorite dress, yellow gingham with little white daisies embroidered on the collar. I must have spent three weeks just doing the embroidery on that collar! 

My eyes were so much better back then, of course. I could thread a needle on the very first try. Now I have to use one of those little wire loop contraptions, and even then, it takes me five minutes and a magnifying glass just to get it through the eye of the needle. Susan wore that yellow dress to her first day of second grade. She had her hair in pigtails with little matching yellow ribbons... oh, she looked just like a little ray of sunshine carrying her tin lunchbox. It had the Peanuts characters on it. Snoopy was always her favorite. 

But wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, being sore or grumpy. No, no, my muscles feel fine, and I'm generally in a very good mood! I just can't seem to stop moving about, that's all.

Weight loss? Oh, heavens no. If anything, I've put on a pound or two since the holidays. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house with the hydrangeas that always look a bit wilted—she brought over this fruitcake. Now, normally I can't stand fruitcake. It's just heavy and tastes like old perfume. But hers had these little candied cherries that reminded me of the ones my mother used to put in her icebox cookies. 

We used to have this big, clunky Frigidaire when I was a girl. The handle was so heavy you had to use two hands to pull it open. It was his favorite tie, too—a horrible mustard yellow thing with little brown ducks on it. I don't know why boys wear such ugly things when they're teenagers. 

But no, I'm not losing weight. And I haven't been sweaty or had my heart race, either. My heart is just fine. I get my blood pressure checked at the pharmacy when I pick up my eye drops, and the machine always says it's perfectly normal. Though those machines are so loud, aren't they? patient.answer:
Bills? Oh heavens, no. I pay my bills the very day they come in the mail. I still write paper checks, you know. My daughter is always pestering me to do it on the iPad, but I just don't trust it. The internet is just floating around in the air, it feels like anyone could just reach up and grab your bank account right out of the sky! I like to sit at my kitchen table with a good pen. I only use blue ink. Black ink always looks so severe, like a collection notice. 

I went to the post office just Tuesday to get a new book of stamps for my envelopes, and they gave me these ones with... oh, what were they... sea cows! Manatees, that's it. Just big gray blobs floating in the water. I asked the clerk—it was a new girl, not Susan. Susan retired to Florida last year to be near her sister who had that terrible hip replacement. Anyway, I asked the new girl if they had any nice flowers or flags, and she just looked at me like I was speaking Greek. Young people today just don't appreciate a pretty piece of mail. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, keeping up with things. No, I don't have any trouble. I write all my doctor appointments on the big calendar on the fridge, right next to the grocery list. And my medications are all sorted in one of those plastic boxes with the little lids that snap shut for the days of the week. Though the 'T' and the 'W' are starting to rub off on mine... I should probably get a new one. Maybe I'll ask David to drive me to the pharmacy later. 

But no, no trouble at all with my memory or my chores. I'm sharp as a tack! I just have these fidgety hands and feet that want to be doing something.

patient.answer:
Medications? Oh, let's see... no, I don't think I take anything at all. No prescriptions, no. I've always been very healthy, praise the Lord. My mother was the same way, you know. She lived to be ninety-two and never took so much as an aspirin. She swore by a hot cup of lemon water every morning and a brisk walk. 

We used to walk down to the bakery on Elm Street. Oh, the smell of that place! They made these little almond cookies that were just heavenly. The baker, Mr. Rossi, was this big, booming Italian man who always wore a white apron covered in flour. He had a parrot in the shop, if you can believe it. A bright green thing that would squawk "Fresh bread! Fresh bread!" whenever the bell above the door rang. I always wondered if it was sanitary, having a bird right there near the pastries, but nobody seemed to mind back then. Things were so different. 

Now, you go into a bakery and everything is wrapped in plastic, and the girls behind the counter look at their phones the whole time. It's just a shame. But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, pills. No, I don't take any. Just a daily vitamin, maybe, when I remember to buy them. But no real medicine. I just have all this pep!

doctor.intent: Assess for classic restless legs syndrome pattern (worse at rest/evening, localized to legs, relieved by movement) versus generalized psychomotor restlessness
doctor.question: Does this restless, need-to-move feeling mainly involve your legs, and does it tend to get worse in the evening or when you're sitting still, then feel better once you get up and move around?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of Restless Legs Syndrome (urge to move legs, worse in evening/at rest, relieved by movement), which is not covered by my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
My legs? Oh, no, it's not just my legs. It's my hands, my arms, my whole body just feels like a motor is running inside me! I don't know about the evening... I feel like this all day long, really. Sitting still is just impossible, whether it's morning, noon, or night. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to sit and watch that nice game show, the one with the spinning wheel? Pat Sajak, he's always so charming. Though I do think Vanna White's dresses have gotten a bit too flashy lately. Back in the eighties, she wore such elegant gowns. My sister Margaret had a dress just like one Vanna wore in 1986—a lovely emerald green silk with a sweetheart neckline. She wore it to her daughter's wedding. 

Oh, that wedding! It was in this beautiful old church with stained glass windows that looked like spun sugar when the sun hit them. But the reception, well, they had a chocolate fountain. A fountain! Can you imagine? Some little boy stuck his whole hand right in it and then wiped it on the white linen tablecloths. His mother was mortified. She was wearing this awful peach pantsuit that just washed her right out. Peach is such a hard color to wear. You really need the right complexion for it. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, moving around. Yes, getting up doesn't really make it go away. I just feel like I need to be doing something constantly. Even when I'm up and walking, I'm tapping my fingers or humming a tune. It's just a constant buzzing feeling everywhere!

patient.answer:
Sad? Oh, heavens no. I haven't been sad at all. If anything, I'm just too full of beans! I haven't lost interest in anything, either. I still love my gardening. I was just out there this morning pulling up weeds around the hydrangeas. 

Hydrangeas are such funny plants, aren't they? You know, you can change the color of the blooms just by putting things in the soil. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house on the corner with the terrible vinyl siding—she puts rusty nails in her soil to make her hydrangeas blue! I told her that sounds like a good way to get lockjaw if you aren't careful with your trowel, but she swears by it. I prefer pink, myself. Pink is such a cheerful color. I had a pink sweater set in the fifties that was just darling. It had these little pearl buttons down the front. I wore it when I met my husband, actually! We were at a church picnic, and he was trying to carry three plates of potato salad at once. 

He dropped one right on my nice white Keds! But he was so apologetic, and he had the bluest eyes... just like Paul Newman. Did you ever see that movie with Paul Newman, the one with the bicycles? Or was it cars? He liked cars, didn't he? He had his own salad dressing, too. I buy the vinaigrette sometimes, it's very tangy. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my mood. No, no, I'm not down in the dumps at all. I just can't seem to stop going and going and going!

Sleep? Oh, well... I've always been a good sleeper, really. I don't think I need any less sleep now than I did before. I still try to get my full eight hours. I like to be in bed by ten o'clock sharp, right after the local news. 

The news is so depressing these days, though, isn't it? It's all just crime and politics. I miss the days when they'd show a nice story about a cat stuck in a tree, and the firemen coming to get it down. Firemen are always so handsome, aren't they? My cousin, Jimmy, he was a fireman back in Chicago. He had this big, thick mustache. All the men had mustaches back then, it was the style! It looked like a caterpillar was resting on his upper lip, I used to tell him. He hated when I said that. 

He married a girl named Betty who made the most wonderful cherry pie. She used real tart cherries, not that syrupy canned stuff. You have to use the tart ones or it's just too sweet. She won a blue ribbon at the state fair for it in 1974. Or was it '75? No, it was '74 because that was the year we had that terrible blizzard and we were snowed in for three days! We just sat around playing Pinochle and eating cherry pie. I never want to see another hand of Pinochle as long as I live! 

But what was the question? Oh, sleep. Yes, I still sleep just fine. I don't wake up feeling like I only need four hours or anything like that. I just... wake up and start buzzing!

Racing thoughts? Well, I don't know if I'd say racing, exactly. I mean, my mind is always busy, of course. There's always something to think about! Like this morning, I was thinking about whether I should make a pot roast for Sunday dinner. 

A good pot roast takes time, you know. You have to sear the meat first to lock in the juices. My mother taught me that. She used this heavy cast-iron skillet that weighed an absolute ton. I don't know how she lifted it, she was such a tiny woman! Barely five feet tall in her stocking feet. She used to buy her shoes in the children's department because her feet were so small. They had these little Mary Janes with a strap across the top... I always wanted a pair like that, but my feet were too wide. 

I had to wear these clunky oxfords when I was a girl. They were so sturdy, they felt like wearing bricks! But my father insisted. He said you needed good arch support or your feet would fall flat as pancakes by the time you were thirty. He was a podiatrist, you see. Dr. Arthur Pendleton. Everyone in town went to him for their corns and bunions. He had this big jar of peppermints on his desk for the children, but they were those chalky ones that tasted like toothpaste. I always preferred butterscotch, myself. Those little yellow candies wrapped in cellophane... they just melt in your mouth! 

But what were we talking about? Oh, my mind jumping around. Well, I suppose I do think about a lot of things, but I wouldn't say my thoughts are racing or out of control. I'm just... thinking! There's just so much to remember, isn't there?

Coffee? Oh, my, no. I haven't had a cup of coffee since... well, it must be twenty years now. It always gave me the most terrible heartburn! And tea, well, I'll have a cup of chamomile before bed sometimes, but that doesn't have any of that caffeine in it. It's very soothing. 

Chamomile reminds me of my Aunt Clara. She used to grow it in her herb garden out back. She had this beautiful little cottage with a thatched roof—can you imagine, a thatched roof in Ohio? The neighbors thought she was absolutely eccentric. She used to dry the herbs by hanging them upside down from the rafters in her kitchen. The whole house smelled like a meadow! She had a parrot, too, named Captain Flint. Oh, that bird was a menace! He used to mimic the sound of the telephone ringing, and poor Aunt Clara would go rushing into the hallway, wiping her hands on her apron, only to find nobody on the line. 

Telephones used to be so heavy, didn't they? The ones with the rotary dial. It took forever to call anyone if they had a lot of nines or zeroes in their number! Click, click, click... and if your finger slipped, you had to hang up and start all over again! Now everyone has those little glass rectangles they poke at. My grandson got me one for Christmas, but I can never remember how to answer it when it rings. It just buzzes and flashes at me like a very angry firefly. 

But what was I saying? Oh, right, caffeine and things. No, I don't take any of those energy things or supplements. Goodness, with how much I'm always buzzing around these days, if I took an energy pill, I think I'd just launch right up into orbit!
